description: By 2100, ocean levels could rise by **one meter**. For entire countries and coastal megacities, this is no longer a distant hypothesis, but a question of planning.

hero.hook: The sea is rising a little more every year, and some countries are already planning their move.

blocks.text: For thousands of years, ocean levels have remained roughly stable. Since the industrial era, it has been climbing, and the speed of this rise is accelerating from year to year.
By 2100, the oceans could rise by 30 centimeters to one meter depending on our emissions choices. For many coastlines, this is no longer a distant threat, but a very concrete planning problem.

Sea levels are rising for two different physical reasons. The first is : when water heats up, its molecules move more and its volume increases a little, like any liquid. The oceans have absorbed more than 90% of the excess heat generated by human activity since 1970, and this heat is increasing their volume. [[Thermal expansion]]

The second reason is the melting of ice placed on dry land. Be careful not to confuse it with the Arctic ice floe, which already floats on the water and whose melting does not cause sea levels to rise. These are the [[Ice sheet]], these immense ice caps placed on the ground of Greenland and Antarctica, which really make the oceans overflow by adding fresh water.

blocks.caption: The melting of Greenland, if it were complete, would raise the oceans by 7 meters.

blocks.text: Greenland loses around 280 billion tonnes of ice each year, or enough water to cover the whole of France with a layer of 50 centimeters.

Since 1880, global sea levels have risen by about 20 centimeters. It is above all the current speed which alarms researchers: it was around 1.4 mm per year in the 20th century, compared to **3.6 mm per year** today, an acceleration of more than 150%.
experts estimate that this trend will continue for decades, even if emissions were drastically reduced now, because the oceans take time to respond to temperature changes. [[IPCC]]

blocks.caption: A rise of 50 cm can turn a 100-year flood into an annual event.

blocks.text: The real danger is not only a slightly higher sea on average, but the multiplication of : a rise of 50 centimeters can be enough to transform a disaster expected once a century into an almost annual event. [[Surges and 100-year floods]]

Rising water levels are mainly affecting regions that have contributed the least to global warming. The large river deltas, such as those of the Nile, the Mekong or the Ganges, are on the front line. In Bangladesh, where 170 million inhabitants live, an increase of one meter could cause the loss of 17% of the territory.

For small island states like the Maldives or Kiribati, disappearing entirely underwater is no longer a science fiction hypothesis, but a real subject of political planning. Conversely, rich megacities like Miami or New York invest billions in dikes and pumps.

blocks.caption: Jakarta combines rising waters and subsidence of the ground, a double threat.

blocks.text: In 2009, the Maldives government held an underwater cabinet meeting in wetsuits to alert the world ahead of a major climate conference.

In **Jakarta**, Indonesia, the city is sinking further into the ground due to excessive pumping of groundwater. Faced with this double threat, the country took the radical decision to build a brand new capital, Nusantara, on the island of Borneo.

Two strategies complement each other in the face of this challenge. The first is to limit warming to slow down the increase beyond 2100. The second is to adapt to what is already inevitable, by strengthening natural defenses like s or dunes, or with heavier solutions like the major works in the Netherlands. [[Mangrove]]

In some cases, the only solution will be to move backwards: moving people and activities inland before disasters repeat themselves too often. This is a real change of habit for societies that have been attached to the coast for centuries.

Sea levels are rising by 3.6 mm per year, under the combined effect of thermal expansion and the melting of land ice. By 2100, this rise could reach one meter and force the displacement of hundreds of millions of people.
